extracted.intended_audience: students, teachers, and readers learning practical criticism and literary critics assessing poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and diagnostic criteria for close reading and judging poems, with an emphasis on common reader errors, technical vs. holistic appraisal, and how various responses (sensory, emotional, doctrinal) affect critical judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty of making out the plain (prose) sense
rubrics_metrics.description: A large proportion of average-to-good readers frequently and repeatedly fail to understand poetry as a statement and as an expression. They fail to make out its prose sense, its plain, overt meaning, taken quite apart from any further poetic significance; and equally they misapprehend its feeling, tone, and intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before moving to 'poetic' readings, attempt to construe the poem as a set of ordinary, intelligible English sentences. Treat failures to grasp literal sense as a significant obstacle to sound criticism; they are not confined to novices and may afflict reputable scholars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensuous apprehension: form, movement, and rhythm
rubrics_metrics.description: Words in sequence have a form to the mind’s ear and tongue; they have a movement and may have a rhythm. There is a wide gulf between readers who immediately perceive this form and movement and those who ignore it or must build it up laboriously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the reader perceives the poem's sound-movement and rhythm naturally. Recognize that the perception of metrical movement is a sensory/intellectual/emotional aptitude and that different readers will experience the verse movement differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place and variability of imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers differ immensely in their capacity to visualise and to produce imagery of other senses. Some minds need images to think; others do not. Poets tend to have exceptional imaging capacity and some readers stress imagery when judging poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about treating images as stable criteria: images aroused in one mind may be wholly different from those in another and may not match any image in the poet’s mind. Avoid judging a poem solely by the images it evokes in you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mnemonic irrelevances (personal associations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Misleading effects arise from the reader being reminded of some personal scene or adventure, erratic associations, or emotional reverberations from a past unrelated to the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try to detect and set aside irrelevant personal memories or associations when they intrude on judgment. Relevance can be difficult to define, but many critical errors stem from such mnemonic intrusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stock responses (pre-programmed reactions)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a poem seems to involve views and emotions already fully prepared in the reader’s mind, the reader's pre-existing record plays, operating quasi- or totally independently of the poem which is supposed to be its origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard against mistaking the reader’s own stock responses for effects produced by the poem. Note when 'the button is pressed' and the response continues irrespective of the poem; in such cases the poem’s credit or blame may be wrongly assigned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentimentality (over-facility of emotional response)
rubrics_metrics.description: An over-facility in certain emotional directions is identified as sentimentality—a peril concerning the due measure of response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether emotional response is proportionate to the poem’s resources. Watch for easy or indulgent emotional reactions that may inflate a poem's apparent value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inhibition / Hardness of Heart
rubrics_metrics.description: Inhibition (sometimes described as Hardness of Heart) is a positive phenomenon that can mask emotional response; it is less studied but must be considered alongside sentimentality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that lack of apparent feeling may reflect inhibition rather than the poem’s insufficiency; evaluate whether a muted response is due to reader disposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrinal adhesions (reader’s beliefs about truth/value)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many poems seem to contain or imply views and beliefs about the world. Questions arise about what bearing the truth-value of those views has upon the worth of the poetry, and whether a reader’s convictions should influence their estimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate the poem’s poetic qualities from agreement or disagreement with its doctrinal claims. Recognize that confusion often stems from treating philosophical or religious content as primary critical ground without examining poetic form or expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical presuppositions and mistaking means for ends
rubrics_metrics.description: When a technique has once been well done we expect it again; conversely, a technique discredited in one context becomes discredited in all. Judging poetry from outside by technical details risks putting means before ends and making blunders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reductive judgments based solely on technical features (e.g., rhyme, stanza-form). Consider how technique serves the poem’s ends rather than assuming fixed rules; do not 'judge pianists by their hair.'

rubrics_metrics.name: General critical preconceptions (theoretical bias)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior demands made upon poetry as a result of conscious or unconscious theories about its nature intervene between the reader and the poem, cutting the reader off from what he may need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be conscious of your own critical theories and how they might filter perception. Try to approach the poem without letting an a priori theory dictate what you will find.

rubrics_metrics.name: Message/doctrine as criterion (truth, originality, profundity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many readers evaluate a poem primarily by the 'message' or doctrine it contains—asking whether the thought is true or false, original or commonplace, profound or obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a poem’s intellectual content, distinguish (a) the truth or novelty of the idea, (b) the skill of expression, and (c) whether a didactic aim is appropriate to the poetic medium. Recognize that reasonable critics may differ widely on these points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression, diction and concision
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgments often turn on whether the poet's thought is clothed fittingly—e.g., concise and clear expression, choice of everyday words, absence of verbal embroidery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how diction and syntax serve the poem’s purpose: does plain speech suit a didactic theme? Does rhetorical phrasing weaken or strengthen concentration? Consider whether the passage gains from verse-form or could be prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metrical qualities and rhythm supporting meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Metre and rhythmic movement can make a 'best possible setting' for a thought, carrying the reader along and conveying tone (e.g., tumbling speech, stress of emotion). The movement experienced depends much on the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether rhythm and metre enhance the poem’s idea and tone (e.g., rugged metre conveying rapid speech or emotion). Note that different readers may hear the movement differently; examine specific line-shapes, sweeps, and accents as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality versus commonplaceness
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics frequently classify an idea as remarkable, commonplace, profound, obvious, original, or trite; originality of thought and freshness of expression are central value-claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether a poem brings fresh treatment to familiar material. Consider whether perceived 'triteness' is a failure of idea or of expression; compare how the same thought is handled by different poets or passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional authenticity versus self-satisfaction or moralizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Some readers perceive genuine noble feeling; others detect self-satisfaction, moralizing, or 'the author’s self-satisfaction' which reduces the poem’s effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate authentic passion from posed or didactic sentiment. Consider whether the poem rouses genuine feeling or merely presents moral aphorisms that produce a sense of self-satisfied propriety in the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagery and metaphorical complexity versus rhetorical or prosaic expression
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem may be praised for vivid imagery and condensation, or criticized as 'prose chopped up to fit a metrical scheme' with rhetorical phrases rather than rich metaphor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the density and appropriateness of images: do they enrich thought or merely ornament it? Beware calling concentrated poetic diction 'prose' without testing how the verse shapes experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intertextual echoes and influence-identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers often judge a passage by its resemblances to other poets (e.g., Wordsworth, Browning) or remembered lines; such comparisons affect reception and interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note legitimate allusions and stylistic echoes, but avoid letting mere resemblance stand in for independent assessment. Use comparative references to illuminate but not to substitute for judgment of the passage itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhyme quality and the temptation to overvalue rhyme
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an exaggerated respect for rhyming ability; readers fix on imperfect rhymes as a tangible test, sometimes ignoring other, more important poetic tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist using rhyme-precision as the sole metric of merit. Consider whether imperfect or partial rhymes were deliberate aesthetic choices and whether rhyme-searching has distracted the poet from higher aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on tangible technical details as a shortcut
rubrics_metrics.description: Features that can be judged without entering the poem—scansion, grammar, descriptive inaccuracy, logical inconsistency—are attractive because they offer definite tests; critics may prefer these 'lapels or buttons' to the ensemble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the convenience of technical critiques but avoid letting them replace a fuller trial of the poem. Use technical points as evidence, not as a substitute for experiencing the poem as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammar and descriptive accuracy checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers may object to specific grammatical or descriptive choices (e.g., tense/verb forms, whether the 'sun can shine shadily'), using these as grounds for condemnation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize such objections: determine whether grammatical oddities are genuine slips or deliberate poetic diction; ask whether apparent descriptive impossibilities are metaphoric and serve the poem’s effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melody, assonance, and musical qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Melody, pace, and musical devices (assonance rather than strict metre) can redeem slightness and heighten simplicity; rhythm and cadence may catch the reader’s heart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate musical qualities both in terms of technical pattern and of felt effect. Consider whether assonance or looser rhythmic patterns are intentionally chosen to produce lyrical simplicity or mood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader’s mood and situational receptivity
rubrics_metrics.description: A reader’s appreciation of a poem can vary with mood and context: a poem may be more appreciated 'in a lighter moment' or when one brings certain experiences to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for situational factors when weighing responses: mark when a favorable or unfavorable reading might be conditioned by the reader’s mood, personal history, or circumstances.
